diagrams.name: poc-p341-lymph-nodes
diagrams.title: Lymphatic system of the head and neck

cloze.text: {{c1::Bulging (exophthalmos)}} or swollen eyes can indicate {{c2::hyperthyroidism}}.
A red {{c1::butterfly-shaped}} lesion over the nose can indicate {{c2::systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)}}.
A {{c1::bulbous}} nose can indicate {{c2::alcohol abuse}}.
cloze.extra: The book writes "ED and a bulbous nose" — "ED" is not explained (probably redness/erythema of the nose).

cloze.text: To examine the TMJ, {{c1::bilaterally}} palpate the joint with both {{c2::index fingers}} while the patient opens and closes the mouth and moves the jaw side to side several times slowly.
During TMJ palpation, note any pain, clicking, popping, {{c1::deviation}}, and {{c2::restriction}} in movements of the mandible.
An enlarged {{c1::masseter}} muscle can indicate {{c2::bruxism and/or clenching}} habits.
When palpating lymph nodes, check for abnormal {{c1::size}}, {{c2::induration}}, and/or {{c3::fixed position}}.
The {{c1::submental}} nodes lie under the chin; the {{c2::submandibular}} nodes lie under the lateral sides of the mandible.
To check the thyroid gland for enlargement and/or immobility, ask the patient to {{c1::swallow}} (may need a glass of water).
Tongue varicosities are {{c1::dark veins}} located {{c2::sublingually}}; more common in {{c3::elderly}} patients and considered {{c4::normal}}.
Fissures of the tongue are grooves that entrap {{c1::food and bacteria}}.
Geographic tongue: affected areas typically present as {{c1::red lesions with white borders}}; the lesions can {{c2::change location}}.
Median rhomboid glossitis: flat, {{c1::red}} smoothness on the {{c2::middle dorsal}} surface of the tongue; related to {{c3::candidiasis}} and patients who are {{c4::immunocompromised}}.
Black hairy tongue: elongation of the {{c1::filiform}} papillae with dark staining.
Black hairy tongue is caused by long-term use of {{c1::metronidazole}}, {{c2::tobacco}}, {{c3::hydrogen peroxide}}, and ingestion of chromogenic food.
The clinician may use {{c1::gauze}} to manipulate the tongue to examine all surfaces; the {{c2::lateral and ventral}} surfaces are the more common areas for oral cancer.
A herpetic lesion appears on {{c1::keratinized}} mucosa, usually forming a {{c2::cluster}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Herpes → H, Keratinized → K: HK → Hong Kong. Herpes is on keratinized tissue, so aphthous ulcers are on non-keratinized tissue.

cloze.text: With an active herpetic lesion, {{c1::postpone treatment}} until the lesion crusts/heals (usually within {{c2::7–10 days}}).
An aphthous ulcer appears on {{c1::non-keratinized}} surfaces such as buccal and labial mucosa, ventral tongue, floor of the mouth, and soft palate.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: HK (Hong Kong) = Herpes on Keratinized, so aphthous = non-keratinized.

cloze.text: Aphthous ulcer lesions are filled, {{c1::white or yellow}}, and surrounded by a {{c2::red halo}}.
{{c1::Petechiae}}: small red dots on mucous membranes caused by trauma or systemic disease.
A {{c1::fistula}} is an opening for infection drainage and may appear as a small, pale, fluid-filled pustule.
{{c1::Linea alba}} appears as a thin white line paralleling the {{c2::occlusal plane}}.
An {{c1::amalgam tattoo}} appears as blue or black macules of varying sizes on soft tissues.
{{c1::Hyperkeratosis}} is a thickening of the tissue, caused by lozenges, drugs, smokeless tobacco, chronic trauma, etc.
Hyperkeratosis from trauma is common on the {{c1::tongue or lip}}; in smokeless tobacco users it is common in the {{c2::vestibules}}.
A tight {{c1::frenum}} attachment can cause loss of attached gingiva, leading to {{c2::recession}} or {{c3::diastema}}.
A {{c1::ranula}} is a soft, bluish, movable enlarged mass on the {{c2::floor of the mouth}}; usually painless.
A ranula involves the {{c1::major}} salivary glands such as the {{c2::submandibular and sublingual}} glands.
A {{c1::mucocele}} is a soft, movable, semi-clear or bluish small swelling, most often on the {{c2::lower lip}} (also gums or palate).
A mucocele involves the {{c1::minor}} salivary glands.
An {{c1::exostosis}} is a small benign bone growth of the alveolar process, mostly on the {{c2::maxillary facial}} surface.
A {{c1::torus}} (plural tori) is a benign bone growth on the {{c2::palate or floor of the mouth}}; it can be unilateral or bilateral.
Tori are not a concern unless a {{c1::partial or full denture}} cannot be fitted.
On palate examination, assess for {{c1::denture}}-related candidiasis, traumas (e.g., "pizza burn"), or signs of {{c2::abuse}}.
In smokers, palatal ducts may appear as {{c1::red dots}} and the palate may be {{c2::"whiter"}} due to physical irritation from smoke.
Assess the shape and height of the palate to adjust the use of the {{c1::radiographic receptor}}.
During teeth evaluation, record open contacts, crowding, malpositioned, rotated, fractured and missing teeth; areas of demineralization or hypocalcification usually appear {{c1::white}}.
Record all {{c1::restorations}}, including bridge, implant, crown, sealant, inlay, onlay, root canal, etc.
{{c1::Attrition}}: loss of tooth structure by {{c2::mechanical forces}} on the occlusal/incisal surfaces.
{{c1::Abrasion}}: loss of tooth structure by mechanical forces {{c2::other than mastication}} (e.g., aggressive brushing, holding a pen in the mouth).

{{c1::Abfraction}}: loss of tooth structure from mechanical stress and flexing of the tooth due to {{c2::occlusal forces}}, usually at the cervical area; usually appears on the cervical third as a {{c3::V-shaped notch}}.
{{c1::Erosion}}: loss of tooth structure by {{c2::chemicals (acids)}}, e.g., excessive vomiting, sucking on lemons, acid reflux.

Angle's classification is based on the relationship of the {{c1::mesiobuccal cusp}} of the permanent {{c2::maxillary first molar}} and the {{c3::buccal groove}} of the permanent {{c4::mandibular first molar}}.
Class I {{c1::neutrocclusion}}: MB cusp of the max 1st molar fits in the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar, with normal overbite and overjet and {{c2::no rotation or crowding}}.
Class I {{c1::malocclusion}}: MB cusp of the max 1st molar fits in the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar, but {{c2::crowding, crossbite, etc.}} is present.
Angle Class II: the MB cusp of the max 1st molar is {{c1::in front of (mesial to)}} the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar.
Angle Class III: the MB cusp of the max 1st molar is {{c1::behind (distal to)}} the buccal groove of the mandibular 1st molar.
Class II Division {{c1::I}}: upper incisors protruded (out). Class II Division {{c2::II}}: upper incisors retruded (in).
Overbite is the {{c1::vertical}} overlap of the maxillary central incisors over the mandibular central incisors.
Overjet is the {{c1::horizontal}} overlap of the maxillary central incisors over the mandibular central incisors.
{{c1::Crossbite}}: teeth are either facial or lingual to their normal position, resulting in "crossover" of the dental arches; it can be {{c2::posterior or anterior}}.
{{c1::Edge-to-edge}}: incisal surfaces of maxillary and mandibular {{c2::anteriors}} occlude instead of overlapping.
{{c1::End-to-end}}: occlusal surfaces of maxillary and mandibular {{c2::posterior}} teeth occlude cusp-to-cusp.
{{c1::Open bite}}: no occlusal contact between teeth that should be in contact.
Note the type of {{c1::orthodontics}} (brackets, clear aligners, retainers) — important for identifying {{c2::plaque-retentive}} areas and modifying oral hygiene instructions.
Document {{c1::appliances}} such as space maintainers, night guards or expanders, as they may affect tissue health and complicate plaque control.
For {{c1::implants}}, record presence and location, assess for {{c2::mucositis or peri-implantitis}}, and avoid using {{c3::metal}} instruments during care.
Identify and chart all {{c1::restorations}} (crowns, fillings, veneers, bridges), noting materials and checking margins for {{c2::overhangs}} or wear.
Document missing teeth and the {{c1::reason}} (extraction, congenital); missing teeth affect occlusion and arch integrity and may lead to {{c2::drifting}}.
Extra teeth (supernumerary) are most common in the {{c1::midline or molar}} region and may interfere with eruption, spacing, or esthetics.
Note unusual shades, white spots or surface defects in color/texture — they may indicate {{c1::hypoplasia}}, {{c2::demineralization}}, or trauma history.

{{c1::Digital (intraoral) scanning}} improves accuracy, enhances patient education, supports treatment planning (restorations, ortho, dentures), and replaces traditional {{c2::impressions}} for better comfort and communication.

{{c1::Delayed}} eruption can be caused by genetics, hormonal imbalances, nutritional deficiencies or medical conditions, e.g., {{c2::hypothyroidism}}, or genetic disorders such as {{c3::ectodermal dysplasia}}.
{{c1::Accelerated}} eruption can be caused by {{c2::hyperthyroidism}}, growth hormone therapy, or medications such as {{c3::phenytoin}} (an anticonvulsant).
Missing teeth (genetic abnormalities or trauma) can lead to {{c1::spacing and alignment}} issues in the remaining teeth.
An {{c1::impacted}} tooth is blocked by bone or teeth (angulation issue); it can cause pain, discomfort and swelling and may require surgical removal or repositioning.
{{c1::Supernumerary}} teeth result from genetic factors or environmental factors such as {{c2::radiation exposure}}; they can lead to crowding and alignment issues.
{{c1::CAMBRA}} (Caries Management By Risk Assessment) classifies patients into caries risk levels and provides targeted interventions.

The CAMBRA recommendations table is designed for {{c1::adult}} patients; for pediatric patients, fluoride concentrations, recall intervals and product use (e.g., CHX) must be adjusted for age and safety.

CAMBRA caries history — low risk: {{c1::no caries in past 3 years}}; moderate: {{c2::no caries but visible risk factors}}; high: {{c3::1 or more cavitated lesions in past 12 months}}; extreme: {{c4::high risk + severe xerostomia}}.

CAMBRA plaque and diet — low risk: minimal plaque, balanced diet; moderate: {{c1::visible plaque, frequent sugar exposure}}; high: {{c2::heavy plaque, frequent snacking}}; extreme: same as high + {{c3::dry mouth worsens sugar clearance}}.
CAMBRA saliva flow — low: normal; moderate: {{c1::slight reduction possible}}; high: may be reduced; extreme: {{c2::severely reduced}} (e.g., radiation, medications, Sjögren's).

CAMBRA protective factors — low: fluoride toothpaste, regular care; moderate: {{c1::inconsistent fluoride, no sealants}}; high: {{c2::inadequate fluoride, no xylitol or varnish use}}; extreme: {{c3::lacks all protective factors, needs saliva support}}.
CAMBRA toothpaste — low and moderate risk: {{c1::OTC fluoride toothpaste 2×/day}}; high and extreme: {{c2::prescription fluoride toothpaste daily}}.
CAMBRA rinse — low: none needed; moderate: optional {{c1::OTC fluoride rinse (NaF)}}; high and extreme: optional short-term {{c2::chlorhexidine rinse}}.
CAMBRA fluoride varnish — low: {{c1::not typically needed}}; moderate: {{c2::every 6 months (optional)}}; high and extreme: {{c3::every 3 months}}.
CAMBRA xylitol — low: optional; moderate: {{c1::gum or mints 2–3×/day}}; high and extreme: {{c2::4–5×/day}}.
CAMBRA sealants — low: {{c1::as needed}}; moderate: {{c2::recommended if deep pits/fissures present}}; high and extreme: {{c3::strongly recommended if not already placed}}.
CAMBRA diet counseling — low: general advice; moderate: {{c1::recommend limiting fermentable carbohydrates}}; high and extreme: {{c2::detailed counseling on sugar frequency and acid exposure}}.
CAMBRA saliva support — low: not needed; moderate: {{c1::monitor only}}; high: {{c2::evaluate if flow appears reduced}}; extreme: {{c3::saliva substitutes, MI Paste, consider physician referral}}.
Decalcified areas can appear (chalky) {{c1::white}}, brown, or black; {{c2::drying}} the tooth may help detect them.
Carious lesions feel {{c1::soft}}; do {{c2::not stab}} the lesion with the explorer.
Use {{c1::transillumination}} (light passes through) to examine dark areas; it can also be used to detect {{c2::calculus}}.
Early childhood caries is mainly present on the {{c1::maxillary anteriors}} because of contact with {{c2::milk}} on those teeth.
{{c1::Arrested}} caries appears brown, smooth, or shiny.
{{c1::Recurrent}} caries can appear as dark shadows surrounding a restoration.
{{c1::Root}} caries appears on root surfaces.
Methamphetamine users may exhibit {{c1::meth mouth}}: severe attrition, erosion, {{c2::rampant caries}}, and mucosal damage.
G.V. Black Class {{c1::I}}: occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth; {{c2::buccal/lingual pits}} of molars and anterior teeth (lingual pits).
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: Class I is not just the occlusal surface of posteriors — it also includes buccal/lingual pits.

cloze.text: G.V. Black Class {{c1::II}}: {{c2::proximal}} surfaces of {{c3::posterior}} teeth.
G.V. Black Class {{c1::III}}: proximal surfaces of anterior teeth {{c2::not involving the incisal edge}}.
G.V. Black Class {{c1::IV}}: proximal surfaces of anterior teeth {{c2::with incisal edge involvement}}.
G.V. Black Class {{c1::V}}: {{c2::gingival third}} of facial or lingual surfaces (anterior and posterior teeth).
G.V. Black Class {{c1::VI}}: {{c2::incisal edges}} of anterior teeth or {{c3::cusp tips}} of posterior teeth.
Radiographic caries Class 1 ({{c1::incipient}}): radiolucency in the {{c2::outer half of enamel}}; {{c3::reversible}} if caught early, no cavitation.
Radiographic caries Class 2 ({{c1::moderate}}): radiolucency extends to the {{c2::inner half of enamel}} but not into dentin; {{c3::remineralization}} possible.
Radiographic caries Class 3 ({{c1::advanced}}): radiolucency into the {{c2::outer third of dentin}}; dentin involvement begins, {{c3::needs restoration}}.
Radiographic caries Class 4 ({{c1::severe}}): radiolucency extends into the {{c2::middle/inner third of dentin}}; extensive damage, usually {{c3::symptomatic}}.
Sealants are {{c1::physical barriers}} that prevent bacteria from collecting in the {{c2::pits and fissures}} of the occlusal, facial and lingual surfaces.
Apply sealants {{c1::before}} applying fluoride varnish, or retention may be affected.
Sealants are {{c1::not necessary}} for adults with low caries risk; they are recommended for {{c2::moderate}} caries risk and up.
Deep occlusal pits and fissures are most prevalent on the {{c1::first and second permanent molars}}; seal molars {{c2::soon after eruption}}.
Sealants are contraindicated for {{c1::open occlusal lesions}} or caries on {{c2::proximal}} surfaces.
Healthy attached gingiva is {{c1::coral pink}} and {{c2::stippled}} (orange-peel appearance); {{c3::melanin pigmentation}} may be present.
In health, the gingival margin fits snugly around the tooth and is positioned {{c1::1–2 mm coronal}} to the CEJ.
In health, interdental papillae fill the embrasure space with a {{c1::knife-edge}} point ({{c2::type I}} embrasure).
In health, the alveolar crest is {{c1::1–2 mm apical}} to the cementoenamel junction (CEJ).
A healthy periodontium has no {{c1::bleeding on probing}} or suppuration, no {{c2::attachment loss}} or mobility, and no furcation involvement because the {{c3::bone level is intact}}.
Gingivitis: {{c1::bright red}} gingiva, rolled gingival margins {{c2::coronal}} to the CEJ, bulbous papillae, {{c3::spongy and edematous}}, and shiny; bleeds upon gentle probing.
Periodontitis: {{c1::pale pink, fibrotic}} gingiva, rolled gingival margins {{c2::apical}} to the CEJ, {{c3::blunted}} papillae, firm and leathery appearance.
In disease, interdental papillae are reduced (type {{c1::II}} embrasure) or lost (type {{c2::III}} embrasure).
Bleeding on gentle probing may be {{c1::reduced}} in periodontitis (fibrotic tissue).
Attachment loss signifies that {{c1::bone destruction}} has occurred; recession, furcation, and mobility may be present.
{{c1::Disclosing solution or tablets}} can be used to stain plaque biofilm for easier visualization during assessment.
Disclosing agents contain dyes that bind to the plaque biofilm's {{c1::extracellular matrix}}.
In two-tone disclosing formulas, {{c1::red}} stains new plaque and {{c2::blue or purple}} stains mature plaque.
Record a {{c1::plaque score}}, communicate it with the patient and repeat at following visits to monitor home-care {{c2::progress}}.
Create achievable plaque-control goals, e.g., reduce the plaque score by {{c1::20%}} for the next re-care visit.
Detect calculus with {{c1::explorers}}, {{c2::radiographs}}, and {{c3::transillumination}}.

Drying with the air-water syringe helps identify calculus: supragingival deposits look {{c1::chalky}} and light in color; subgingival deposits look {{c2::darker}} (blood pigments are absorbed into the calculus).
To assess mobility, use the {{c1::blunt ends}} of instruments on opposite sides of the tooth, rock {{c2::horizontally}}, then press {{c3::vertically}} with one end of the mirror handle.
Tooth mobility is recorded with the {{c1::Miller}} classification.
Miller mobility Class {{c1::I}}: facial-lingual horizontal displacement up to {{c2::1 mm}}.
Miller mobility Class {{c1::II}}: facial-lingual horizontal displacement {{c2::greater than 1 mm, up to 2 mm}}.
Miller mobility Class {{c1::III}}: horizontal displacement {{c2::more than 2 mm}} and/or {{c3::vertical displacement (depression into the socket)}}.

basic.front: Chapping and angular cheilitis of the lips can indicate what? (5 causes)
basic.back: Mouth breathing, nutritional deficiency, purging habits, excessive sun exposure, or fungal infection
Disease of the lymph nodes that includes enlargement

basic.front: Geographic tongue is also known as …
Median rhomboid glossitis is also known as …
What is myofunctional therapy, and when can it help a frenectomy patient?
basic.back: Targeted exercises for the lips, tongue and orofacial muscles; done before or after a frenectomy it can improve function, promote proper tongue posture and enhance outcomes.
basic.extra: Did you know? Some dental hygienists became oral myofunctional therapists.

basic.front: In a case study with missing teeth, why does the reason for the tooth loss matter?
basic.back: If even one tooth was lost due to periodontitis, AAP staging jumps to Stage III or IV. Loss from malformation, infection, orthodontics or other reasons does not change the stage.
basic.extra: Board Alert: checking for missing teeth and asking why is one of the first things to do in a case study.

basic.front: How do you tell a Class I buccal-pit lesion from a Class V buccal lesion?
basic.back: Class I = a pit, an indentation more toward the middle of the buccal surface; Class V = along the gingival margin (gingival third).

basic.front: Two-tone disclosing: why does new plaque stain red and mature plaque blue/purple?
basic.back: New plaque is loosely organized and high in water, so it absorbs the red dye quickly; mature plaque is denser with more bacterial byproducts that trap the darker dye molecules.

typein.question: Normal overbite: how many mm? (format: a–b mm)
Normal overbite as a percentage of the lower incisor covered? (format: a–b%)
Overjet greater than how many mm is considered excessive?
AAP 2017: tooth loss due to periodontitis of how many teeth or more = Stage IV?
typein.extra: Stage III = loss of up to 4 teeth due to periodontitis.

typein.question: How many CAMBRA caries-risk levels are there in the book's table?
CAMBRA: OTC fluoride toothpaste for low-risk adults contains how many ppm? (format: a–b)
CAMBRA: prescription fluoride toothpaste for high/extreme risk contains how many ppm NaF?
CAMBRA: concentration of the OTC NaF rinse for moderate risk? (in %)
CAMBRA: concentration of the short-term chlorhexidine rinse for high risk? (in %)
CAMBRA: total daily xylitol for high-risk adults? (format: a–b g/day)
CAMBRA recall interval for HIGH-risk adults? (format: a–b months)
CAMBRA recall interval for MODERATE-risk adults? (format: a–b months)
A probing depth of at least how many mm forms a pocket? (format: N mm)
typein.extra: Probing depth 4 mm+ = pocket; 1–3 mm = sulcus.

items: Inner half of enamel, not into dentin (moderate)

Sort these findings: gingivitis or periodontitis?

mcq.question: An HIV-positive patient has a flat, smooth, red, diamond-shaped area in the middle of the dorsal tongue that does not change location between visits. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Median rhomboid glossitis (central papillary atrophy) is a flat red smooth area on the middle dorsal tongue, linked to candidiasis and immunocompromise. Geographic tongue also shows red areas, but they have white borders and change location.

mcq.question: A patient reports a painful lesion that appeared two days ago. Clinically you see a cluster of small ulcerated vesicles on the attached gingiva. What is the best action?
options: A. Proceed with scaling, avoiding the area
B. Postpone treatment until the lesion crusts/heals
C. Apply topical anesthetic and proceed
D. Refer for biopsy before any care
mcq.answer: B. Postpone treatment until the lesion crusts/heals
mcq.explanation: Clustered lesions on keratinized tissue (attached gingiva) are herpetic; treatment is postponed until the lesion crusts/heals, usually within 7–10 days. An aphthous ulcer would be single, on non-keratinized mucosa, with a red halo.

mcq.question: A child has a soft, painless, bluish, movable swelling on the floor of the mouth to one side of the tongue. Which glands are most likely involved?
mcq.explanation: A bluish movable mass on the floor of the mouth is a ranula, which involves major salivary glands (submandibular and sublingual). A mucocele looks similar but usually on the lower lip and involves minor salivary glands.

mcq.question: An adult patient had two cavitated lesions restored 8 months ago and has normal salivary flow. Per CAMBRA, which home-care recommendation fits her risk level?
options: A. OTC fluoride toothpaste (1,000–1,500 ppm) 2×/day only
B. Prescription 5,000 ppm NaF toothpaste daily
C. Saliva substitutes and MI Paste
mcq.answer: B. Prescription 5,000 ppm NaF toothpaste daily
mcq.explanation: ≥1 cavitated lesion in the past 12 months = high risk; high risk gets prescription 5,000 ppm NaF toothpaste daily (plus varnish every 3 months). Saliva substitutes/MI Paste are for extreme risk (high risk + severe xerostomia), which she does not have.

mcq.question: A bitewing shows a proximal radiolucency reaching the inner half of the enamel but not the DEJ. Which is the most appropriate statement?
options: A. It is incipient and limited to the outer enamel
C. Dentin is involved and it needs restoration
mcq.explanation: Radiolucency in the inner half of enamel but not dentin = Class 2 (moderate), where remineralization is possible. Restoration is needed once the radiolucency reaches the outer third of dentin (Class 3).

mcq.question: Which tooth is the BEST candidate for a sealant?
options: A. A newly erupted permanent first molar with deep fissures in a moderate-risk child
B. A molar with an open occlusal carious lesion
C. A premolar with proximal caries
D. Any molar of a low-risk adult
mcq.answer: A. A newly erupted permanent first molar with deep fissures in a moderate-risk child
mcq.explanation: Deep pits and fissures of 1st/2nd permanent molars should be sealed soon after eruption; sealants are recommended for moderate risk and up. They are contraindicated for open occlusal lesions or proximal caries, and not necessary for low-risk adults.

mcq.question: Which finding confirms that periodontitis rather than gingivitis is present?
mcq.explanation: Attachment loss signifies bone destruction has occurred — the defining feature of periodontitis. Bleeding, bulbous papillae and bright red shiny tissue are gingivitis signs (bleeding may even be reduced in fibrotic periodontitis).

mcq.question: A tooth moves 1.5 mm facial-lingually and cannot be depressed into the socket. What is its Miller mobility class?
mcq.explanation: Class II = horizontal displacement greater than 1 mm up to 2 mm. Class III requires more than 2 mm or vertical displacement (depression into the socket).
